paragraphs:
Here a godless crowd of torturers long fed their fury,
Never satisfied with innocent blood.
Now the homeland is safe and the den of death destroyed:
Where dreadful death once ruled, life and safety stand open.
[Four-line verse composed for the gates of a market planned for the site of the Jacobin Club House in Paris.]

I was sick—sick to death from that long agony. When at last they untied me and allowed me to sit, I felt my senses leaving me. The sentence—the dreadful sentence of death—was the last clearly spoken thing that reached my ears. After that, the voices of the Inquisition seemed to merge into one dreamy, indistinct hum. It brought to my soul the idea of something turning round and round—perhaps because my imagination associated it with the whirring of a mill wheel. This lasted only briefly, for soon I heard nothing more. Yet for a while I could see—but how terribly everything was exaggerated! I saw the lips of the judges in their black robes. They seemed white—whiter than the paper on which I am writing these words—and grotesquely thin. Their thinness expressed an intensity of firmness, of unshakeable determination, of stern contempt for human suffering under torture. I saw that the decrees of what, to me, was Fate were still coming from those lips. I saw them twist as they formed their deadly words. I saw them shape the syllables of my name, and shuddered because no sound followed. For a few moments of delirious horror, I also saw the soft, almost imperceptible movement of the black draperies covering the room’s walls. Then my eyes fell on the seven tall candles on the table. At first they looked merciful, like slender white angels who would save me. But suddenly a deadly nausea swept over my spirit. Every fibre of my body shuddered as though I had touched the wire of an electric battery. The angel shapes became meaningless ghosts with heads of flame, and I saw that they could offer no help. Then, like a rich musical note, the thought slipped into my imagination of the sweet rest there must be in the grave. It came gently and secretly, and seemed to take a long time to make its full impression. But just as my soul finally began to feel and accept it, the judges’ figures vanished before me as if by magic. The tall candles dwindled into nothing; their flames went out completely; utter blackness followed. Every sensation seemed swallowed in a mad, rushing descent, like a soul plunging into Hades. Then silence, stillness and night were the whole universe.

I had fainted, but I will not say that I had lost all consciousness. I will not try to define or even describe what remained; still, it was not all lost. In the deepest sleep—no! In delirium—no! In a faint—no! In death—no! Even in the grave, not everything is lost. Otherwise there is no immortality for humanity. Waking from the deepest sleep, we break the fine, fragile web of a dream. Yet a second later, so delicate may that web have been, we do not even remember dreaming. There are two stages in returning to life from a faint. First comes the sense of existing mentally or spiritually; second, the sense of existing physically. It seems likely that, if we could remember the first stage’s impressions once we reached the second, those impressions would speak vividly of memories from the gulf beyond. And what is that gulf? How, at least, can we distinguish its shadows from those of the tomb? Even if we cannot deliberately recall the impressions of what I have called the first stage, do they not return uninvited after long intervals, leaving us wondering where they came from? A man who has never fainted is not the one who finds strange palaces and wildly familiar faces in glowing coals. He is not the one who sees sad visions floating in the air, unseen by most people; not the one who broods over the scent of an unfamiliar flower; not the one whose mind becomes bewildered by the meaning of a musical phrase that has never caught his attention before.

During my many thoughtful attempts to remember, my earnest struggles to recover some trace of the apparent nothingness into which my soul had fallen, there have been moments when I imagined I had succeeded. There have been brief, very brief periods when I have summoned memories that, in the clear reasoning of a later time, I am certain could refer only to that state of apparent unconsciousness. These shadowy memories tell indistinctly of tall figures lifting me and carrying me silently down—down—still down. The mere idea that the descent would never end filled me with a hideous dizziness. They also tell of a vague horror in my heart because that heart was so unnaturally still. Then comes a sense that everything has suddenly stopped moving. It is as though those carrying me—a ghastly procession!—had descended beyond the limits of the limitless, and paused, exhausted by their labour. After that I remember flatness and dampness. Then everything is madness—the madness of a memory occupied with forbidden things.

Very suddenly, movement and sound returned to my soul: the violent movement of my heart and, in my ears, the sound of its beating. Then a pause in which everything is blank. Then sound again, and movement, and touch—a tingling sensation throughout my body. Then the mere awareness of existing, without thought—a state that lasted a long time. Then, very suddenly, thought, shuddering terror, and an earnest effort to understand my true situation. Then a powerful wish to fall back into unconsciousness. Then a rushing revival of my soul and a successful effort to move. And now a complete memory of the trial, the judges, the black draperies, the sentence, the sickness, the fainting. Then a total blank concerning everything that followed—everything that, in later days, determined efforts have allowed me vaguely to recall.

So far I had not opened my eyes. I felt that I was lying on my back, untied. I reached out a hand, and it fell heavily on something damp and hard. I left it there for many minutes while I tried to imagine where I could be and what had happened to me. I longed to look, but dared not. I dreaded my first glimpse of the things around me. It was not that I feared seeing something horrible; I was terrified there might be nothing to see. At last, with wild desperation in my heart, I opened my eyes quickly. My worst fears were confirmed. The blackness of eternal night surrounded me. I struggled for breath. The sheer darkness seemed to press upon me and suffocate me. The air was unbearably stuffy. Still lying quietly, I tried to use my reason. I recalled the proceedings of the Inquisition and attempted to work out my actual situation from there. The sentence had been passed, and it seemed that a very long time had elapsed since then. Yet I never supposed, even for a moment, that I was actually dead. Whatever we may read in fiction, that idea is completely incompatible with being alive. But where was I, and in what condition? I knew that those condemned to death usually perished at the Inquisition’s public religious ceremonies. One of these had taken place on the very night of my trial. Had I been sent back to my dungeon to await the next sacrifice, which would not happen for many months? I immediately saw that this was impossible. Victims had been needed at once. Besides, my dungeon, like every condemned cell in Toledo, had a stone floor and was not completely shut off from light.

A terrifying idea suddenly sent the blood rushing to my heart, and for a little while I lost consciousness again. On recovering, I immediately sprang to my feet, every fibre of my body shaking violently. I thrust my arms wildly above and around me in every direction. I felt nothing, but I was afraid to take a step in case the walls of a tomb should block my way. Sweat burst from every pore and stood in large, cold beads on my forehead. At last the agony of not knowing became unbearable. I moved cautiously forward with my arms stretched out and my eyes straining from their sockets, hoping to catch some faint ray of light. I went many paces, but there was still only darkness and emptiness. I breathed more freely. It seemed clear that, at least, I had not suffered the most hideous fate of all.

As I continued to step cautiously forward, a thousand vague rumours about the horrors of Toledo crowded into my memory. Strange things had been told about its dungeons. I had always thought them fables, but they were strange all the same, and too ghastly to repeat except in a whisper. Had I been left to starve in this underground world of darkness? Or did some other, perhaps still more terrible fate await me? I knew my judges’ character too well to doubt that the end would be death, and a death more bitter than usual. Only its manner and its hour occupied and tormented my mind.

At last my outstretched hands met a solid obstacle. It was a wall, apparently made of stone: very smooth, slimy and cold. I followed it, taking every step with the wary suspicion those old accounts had taught me. But this gave me no way to establish the dungeon’s size. The wall seemed so completely uniform that I might go all the way round and return to my starting point without knowing it. I therefore searched for the knife that had been in my pocket when they led me into the Inquisition’s chamber. It was gone. My clothes had been replaced with a robe of coarse woollen cloth. I had meant to force the blade into some tiny crack in the masonry to mark where I had started. This difficulty was really trivial, although in my confused state it at first seemed impossible to overcome. I tore a strip from the robe’s hem and laid it out at full length, at a right angle to the wall. As I felt my way round the prison, I could not fail to find this rag when I completed the circuit. So, at least, I thought. But I had not allowed for the size of the dungeon or my own weakness. The ground was damp and slippery. I staggered on for some time, then stumbled and fell. Utter exhaustion made me stay where I had fallen, and soon I was asleep.

On waking and stretching out an arm, I found a loaf and a jug of water beside me. I was too exhausted to wonder about this, and ate and drank greedily. Soon afterwards I continued my journey round the prison. After much effort I finally reached the strip of woollen cloth. Before falling, I had counted fifty-two paces. Since beginning to walk again I had counted another forty-eight before reaching the rag. That made a hundred paces altogether. Allowing two paces to a yard, I estimated that the dungeon measured fifty yards round. But I had encountered many corners in the wall, so I could not guess the shape of the vaulted chamber, which I could not help assuming it was.

I had little purpose—and certainly no hope—in these investigations, but a vague curiosity urged me to continue. Leaving the wall, I decided to cross the room. At first I moved with extreme caution. Although the floor seemed solid, it was treacherously slimy. Eventually, however, I grew bolder and began stepping firmly, trying to cross in as straight a line as possible. I had gone some ten or twelve paces when what remained of the robe’s torn hem became tangled between my legs. I stepped on it and fell violently on my face.

Confused by the fall, I did not immediately notice a rather startling fact. A few seconds later, while I was still lying flat, it caught my attention. My chin rested on the prison floor, but my lips and the upper part of my head touched nothing, although they seemed lower than my chin. At the same time, a clammy mist seemed to bathe my forehead, and the peculiar smell of rotting fungus rose into my nostrils. I stretched an arm forward and shuddered. I had fallen at the very edge of a circular pit, whose size I naturally had no way to establish just then. Feeling about the masonry just below its rim, I managed to loosen a small fragment and dropped it into the abyss. For many seconds I listened to the echoes as it struck the sides of the chasm on its way down. At last there was a dull splash into water, followed by loud echoes. At that same moment I heard something like a door overhead being quickly opened and shut again. A faint gleam of light suddenly flashed through the gloom, then just as suddenly vanished.

I now clearly understood the doom prepared for me, and congratulated myself on the timely accident that had saved me from it. One more step before I fell, and the world would have seen me no more. The death I had just avoided was precisely the kind I had dismissed as an idle invention in stories about the Inquisition. The victims of its tyranny faced a choice: death with the worst physical agonies, or death with the most hideous mental horrors. I had been reserved for the latter. Long suffering had shattered my nerves until I trembled at the sound of my own voice. In every respect, I had become a suitable victim for the kind of torture awaiting me.

Shaking in every limb, I felt my way back to the wall. I resolved to die there rather than risk the terrors of the pits, which I now imagined scattered throughout the dungeon. In a different state of mind, I might have had the courage to end my misery at once by plunging into one of these abysses. Now I was an absolute coward. Nor could I forget what I had read about these pits: a sudden end to life was no part of their most horrible design.

My agitation kept me awake for many long hours, but eventually I slept again. On waking I found, as before, a loaf and a jug of water beside me. A burning thirst consumed me, and I emptied the jug in a single draught. It must have been drugged, for I had scarcely drunk before an irresistible drowsiness came over me. I fell into a deep sleep—a sleep like death. How long it lasted, of course, I do not know. But when I opened my eyes again, I could see the things around me. A strange sulphurous glow, whose source I could not at first discover, revealed the size and appearance of the prison.

I had been very wrong about its size. Its walls measured no more than twenty-five yards all the way round. For several minutes this fact caused me a great deal of useless concern—useless indeed! In the terrible circumstances surrounding me, what could matter less than the mere dimensions of my dungeon? But my mind took a frantic interest in trifles, and I occupied myself by trying to explain my mistaken measurement. At last the truth flashed upon me. During my first exploration, I had counted fifty-two paces before I fell. I must then have been within a pace or two of the strip of cloth. In fact, I had almost completed the circuit. I had then slept, and on waking must have retraced my steps, which made me imagine the circuit was nearly twice its actual length. My confusion had prevented me from noticing that I began with the wall on my left and finished with it on my right.

I had also been mistaken about the room’s shape. While feeling my way round, I had found many corners and concluded that its outline was very irregular. Such is the power of total darkness over someone emerging from a stupor or sleep! The corners were merely a few shallow recesses or niches at uneven intervals. The prison’s overall shape was square. What I had taken for masonry now seemed to be iron, or some other metal, in enormous sheets. Their seams or joints formed the recesses. The entire metal surface was crudely painted with all the hideous, repulsive images produced by the monks’ superstitions about death and the grave. Threatening demons, skeletal figures, and other still more frightening images covered and disfigured the walls. I noticed that their outlines were clear enough, but their colours seemed faded and blurred, as though by damp air. I now also noticed that the floor was stone. In the centre gaped the circular pit from whose jaws I had escaped. It was the dungeon’s only pit.

I saw all this indistinctly and with great effort, for my own situation had changed considerably while I slept. I now lay flat on my back on a sort of low wooden framework. I was securely fastened to it by a long strap like one fastened round a horse’s body. It wound many times round my limbs and body, leaving only my head free, and my left arm able to move just enough that, with great effort, I could feed myself from an earthenware dish on the floor beside me. To my horror, I saw that the water jug had been removed. I say to my horror because an intolerable thirst consumed me. My tormentors seemed intent on making that thirst worse: the dish contained strongly seasoned meat.

Looking up, I examined the prison’s ceiling. It was some thirty or forty feet above me, and built much like the walls. A very peculiar figure in one panel seized all my attention. It was a painting of Time, in his usual form, except that instead of a scythe he held what, at a glance, I took for a painted image of an enormous pendulum like those on old clocks. Something about this machine’s appearance, however, made me study it more closely. As I gazed straight upwards—it was directly over me—I thought I saw it moving. A moment later I knew that I had. Its swing was short and, of course, slow. I watched for several minutes, with some fear but greater wonder. Eventually, tired of watching its monotonous movement, I turned my eyes to the other things in the cell.

A slight noise caught my attention. Looking at the floor, I saw several enormous rats crossing it. They had come out of the pit, which was just within sight on my right. Even as I watched, they hurried up in groups, their eyes ravenous, drawn by the smell of the meat. Scaring them away from it took considerable effort and attention.

Perhaps half an hour passed, perhaps even an hour—I could judge time only very imperfectly—before I looked up again. What I saw bewildered and astonished me. The pendulum’s swing had widened by nearly a yard. Naturally, its speed had also increased considerably. But what disturbed me most was the realisation that it had noticeably descended. I now saw, with a horror I need hardly describe, that its lower end was a crescent of glittering steel, about a foot from tip to tip. The tips pointed upwards, and the lower edge was evidently as sharp as a razor. Like a razor, too, it looked solid and heavy, widening from its cutting edge into a broad, thick body above. It hung from a heavy brass rod, and the whole thing hissed as it swung through the air.

I could no longer doubt the fate prepared for me by the monks’ ingenuity in torture. The Inquisition’s agents had learned that I knew about the pit—that pit whose horrors had been intended for a religious dissenter as bold as I was; that pit which symbolised hell and was rumoured to be the ultimate extreme of all their punishments. I had avoided falling into it by the slightest accident. I knew that surprising victims, or trapping them into torment, was an important part of the grotesque business of killing people in these dungeons. Since I had not fallen, throwing me into the abyss was no part of their demonic plan. With no other alternative, a different and milder destruction awaited me. Milder! I half smiled in my agony at applying such a word to such a thing.

What good would it do to describe the long, long hours of more than human horror during which I counted the steel’s rushing swings? Inch by inch—fraction by fraction—it descended, so slowly that I could notice its progress only at intervals that seemed like ages. Down, and still down, it came! Days passed—perhaps many days passed—before it swept close enough to fan me with its biting breath. The smell of the sharp steel forced its way into my nostrils. I prayed—I exhausted heaven with prayers for it to descend faster. I became frantically mad and struggled to thrust myself upwards against the fearful curved sword as it swept past. Then I suddenly grew calm, and lay smiling at the glittering death as a child smiles at a rare trinket.

There was another period of complete unconsciousness. It was brief, for when I came back to life the pendulum had not noticeably descended. But it might have been long. I knew there were demons watching me faint, who could stop the swinging whenever they pleased. On recovering, too, I felt very—oh, indescribably—sick and weak, as though from prolonged starvation. Even amid the agonies of that time, human nature craved food. With painful effort I stretched my left arm as far as my bonds allowed and took the little food the rats had left me. As I put some between my lips, a half-formed thought of joy—of hope—rushed into my mind. Yet what business had I with hope? It was, as I say, a half-formed thought. We have many such thoughts that are never completed. I felt that it promised joy, hope, but also that it had died while forming. In vain I struggled to complete it—to recover it. Long suffering had almost destroyed all my ordinary mental powers. I was an imbecile—an idiot.

The pendulum swung at a right angle across the length of my body. I saw that the crescent was meant to pass over my heart. It would fray the woollen cloth of my robe; it would return and repeat its work—again—and again. Despite the terrifying width of its swing, some thirty feet or more, and the hissing force of its descent, powerful enough to split these very iron walls, for several minutes it would do no more than fray my robe. At that thought I stopped. I dared not think beyond it. I concentrated stubbornly on it, as though by doing so I could halt the steel’s descent at that point. I forced myself to consider the sound the crescent would make as it passed across the garment, and the peculiar shivering sensation that the rubbing of cloth produces in the nerves. I thought about these trivial things until they set my teeth on edge.

Down—steadily down it crept. I took a frantic pleasure in comparing the speed of its descent with the speed of its sideways movement. To the right—to the left—far and wide—with the shriek of a damned spirit! Towards my heart with the stealthy pace of a tiger! I laughed and howled by turns as one idea or the other took hold of me.

Down—certainly, relentlessly down! It swung within three inches of my chest! I struggled violently, furiously, to free my left arm. Only the part from elbow to hand was free. With great effort I could move my hand from the dish beside me to my mouth, but no further. If I could have broken the bindings above my elbow, I would have seized the pendulum and tried to stop it. I might as well have tried to stop an avalanche!

Down—still without stopping—still inevitably down! I gasped and struggled at every swing. I shrank back convulsively each time it swept past. My eyes followed its outward or upward movement with the eager attention of utterly futile despair. They shut involuntarily when it descended, although death would have been a relief—oh, an indescribable relief! Yet every nerve quivered at the thought of how little further the machinery needed to sink to bring that sharp, glittering axe down upon my chest. Hope made my nerves tremble and my body shrink away. It was hope—the hope that triumphs on the torture rack, that whispers to those condemned to death even in the dungeons of the Inquisition.

I saw that another ten or twelve swings would bring the steel into actual contact with my robe. With that observation, all the sharp, controlled calm of despair suddenly came over me. For the first time in many hours—or perhaps days—I thought. It now occurred to me that the strap wrapped round me was a single piece. No separate cord tied me down. The first stroke of the razor-sharp crescent across any part of that strap would cut it so that I could unwind it from my body with my left hand. But how terrifyingly close the steel would be! The slightest struggle would be fatal! Besides, was it likely that the torturer’s servants had failed to foresee this possibility and guard against it? Was it likely that the strap crossed my chest in the pendulum’s path? Afraid to see this faint hope—which seemed my last—defeated, I raised my head just far enough to get a clear view of my chest. The strap bound my limbs and body tightly in every direction except the path of the destroying crescent.

Scarcely had I lowered my head again when something flashed into my mind. I can best describe it as the missing half of that idea of escape I mentioned earlier, only half of which had drifted vaguely through my mind when I raised food to my burning lips. The whole thought was there now—feeble, barely sane, barely definite, but complete. At once, with the nervous energy of despair, I tried to put it into action.

For many hours, the area immediately around the low framework on which I lay had been literally swarming with rats. They were wild, bold and ravenous. Their red eyes glared at me as though they waited only for me to stop moving before making me their prey. ‘What food,’ I thought, ‘have they grown used to down in the pit?’

Despite all my efforts to prevent them, they had devoured everything in the dish except a small remnant. I had fallen into the habit of waving my hand back and forth around the dish. Eventually the unconscious regularity of this movement made it useless. In their hunger, the vermin often sank their sharp teeth into my fingers. With the scraps of oily, spicy meat that remained, I rubbed the strap thoroughly wherever I could reach it. Then I lifted my hand from the floor and lay breathlessly still.

At first the ravenous animals were startled and terrified by the change—by the end of all movement. They drew back in alarm, and many retreated to the pit. But only for a moment. I had not relied on their hunger in vain. Seeing that I remained still, one or two of the boldest leapt onto the framework and sniffed at the strap. This seemed to signal a general rush. Fresh groups hurried out of the pit. They clung to the wood, overran it, and leapt onto my body in hundreds. The pendulum’s regular movement did not disturb them at all. Dodging its strokes, they busied themselves with the greased strap. They pressed and swarmed over me in ever-growing heaps. They writhed across my throat. Their cold lips sought mine. I was half suffocated by the pressure of their crowds. A disgust for which the world has no name swelled in my chest and chilled my heart with a heavy, clammy coldness. Yet I felt that in one more minute the struggle would be over. I could plainly feel the strap loosening. I knew it must already be cut through in more than one place. With more than human determination, I lay still.

My calculations had not been wrong, and I had not endured it in vain. At last I felt that I was free. The strap hung in ribbons from my body. But the pendulum’s stroke was already pressing against my chest. It had cut through the woollen robe. It had cut through the linen beneath. Twice more it swung, and a sharp pain shot through every nerve. But the moment of escape had come. A wave of my hand sent my rescuers rushing away in confusion. With a steady movement—cautious, sideways, shrinking and slow—I slid out of the strap’s embrace and beyond the curved sword’s reach. For the moment, at least, I was free.

Free! And still in the Inquisition’s grasp! I had scarcely stepped from my wooden bed of horror onto the prison’s stone floor when the hellish machine stopped moving. I saw it drawn up through the ceiling by some invisible force. This lesson sank into me with desperate force. There could be no doubt that every movement I made was being watched. Free! I had only escaped one agonising form of death to be delivered into something worse than death in another form. At that thought my eyes darted nervously round the iron barriers enclosing me. Clearly something unusual had happened in the room—some change I could not at first make out. For many minutes, trembling and lost in a dreamlike distraction, I occupied myself with useless, disconnected guesses. During this time I became aware, for the first time, of where the sulphurous light illuminating the cell came from. It shone through a gap about half an inch wide that ran all the way round the prison at the base of the walls. The walls thus appeared to be, and actually were, completely separate from the floor. I tried to look through this opening, but of course I could not.

As I rose from that attempt, I suddenly understood the mysterious change in the room. I have mentioned that although the outlines of the figures on the walls were clear enough, their colours looked blurred and indistinct. Those colours had now become startlingly, intensely brilliant, and were growing brighter every moment. They gave the images of ghosts and demons an appearance that might have shaken even stronger nerves than mine. Demonic eyes, full of wild and ghastly life, glared at me from a thousand directions where none had been visible before. They gleamed with the lurid brightness of a fire I could not force my imagination to consider unreal.

Unreal! Even as I breathed, the fumes of heated iron reached my nostrils! A suffocating smell filled the prison! Each moment the eyes glaring at my agonies glowed more deeply! A richer crimson spread over the painted horrors of blood. I panted! I gasped for breath! There could be no doubt of my tormentors’ intention—oh, those most relentless men! Oh, those most demonic men! I shrank away from the glowing metal towards the centre of the cell. Amid the thought of the fiery destruction threatening me, the idea of the pit’s coolness came like a balm to my soul. I rushed to its deadly edge. I strained my eyes downwards. The glare from the glowing roof lit its deepest recesses. Yet for one frantic moment my mind refused to grasp what I saw. At last its meaning forced its way in—wrestled its way into my soul—burned itself into my shuddering reason. Oh, for a voice to speak! Oh, horror! Oh, any horror but this! With a shriek I rushed from the edge, buried my face in my hands, and wept bitterly.

The heat increased rapidly. Once more I looked up, shaking as though with a violent fever. A second change had taken place in the cell, and this time its shape was clearly changing. As before, at first I tried in vain to grasp or understand what was happening. But I was not left uncertain for long. My double escape had hurried the Inquisition’s revenge. There would be no more playing with the King of Terrors. The room had been square. Now I saw that two of its iron corners had become narrower than right angles, and the other two wider. The dreadful change increased rapidly with a low rumbling or moaning sound. In an instant, the room had become a diamond. But the transformation did not stop there. I neither hoped nor wished that it would. I could have clasped the red-hot walls to my chest like a garment of eternal peace. ‘Death,’ I said, ‘any death except death in the pit!’ Fool! Should I not have known that the burning iron was meant to drive me into the pit? Could I withstand its heat? Even if I could, could I withstand its pressure? The diamond grew flatter and flatter, so quickly that I had no time to think. Its centre, and therefore its widest part, lay directly above the gaping gulf. I shrank back, but the closing walls forced me irresistibly forward. At last there was not an inch of firm prison floor left to support my scorched, writhing body. I struggled no more. The agony of my soul burst out in one loud, long, final scream of despair. I felt myself tottering on the edge. I turned my eyes away—

There was a discordant hum of human voices! There was a loud blast like many trumpets! There was a harsh grinding like a thousand thunderclaps! The fiery walls rushed backwards! An outstretched arm caught mine as I fell, fainting, into the abyss. It was General Lasalle’s arm. The French army had entered Toledo. The Inquisition was in its enemies’ hands.
